The trouble goes well beyond Anthropic: Nasdaq stocks lost more than $4 trillion in value this week, erasing the index’s gains for the year .

   Behind Anthropic’s debut are siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who have built a company that prides itself on being anything but ordinary. Our reporters take you inside the brother-sister partnership at the top of what’s still one of the world’s most valuable companies.

       2. TODAY’S HEADLINES   • The White House plans to scale back its use of “special government employees,” who can work for the government while retaining their private-sector salaries or investments.

   • New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have forged an unlikely partnership that has helped keep crime low and reassured business and Jewish community leaders. Making it work has required compromises.

   • A California jury found a man guilty of intentionally sparking the 2025 fire that devastated Los Angeles’s Pacific Palisades.

   • Citadel Chief Executive Ken Griffin spent at least five years courting elite universities to bring a top technology school to Miami, hoping to turn his new home into a global business hub . He ultimately struck a $3 billion deal with Carnegie Mellon University.

   • Denmark said it would expel Russia’s defense attaché after accusing Moscow of ordering the attempted killing of a Ukrainian-American rapper on Danish soil.

   • Here’s a visual look at how El Salvador President Nayib Bukele is taking his gang-fighting strategy to Haiti .

       3. FROM THE MARKETS   • Activist billionaire Nelson Peltz wants to take Wendy’s private . But the struggling burger chain’s CEO Bob Wright is standing in his way.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   France’s riots are testing its colorblind ideals.   Student protests over school conditions spiraled into riots, setting off a fierce debate over who was responsible. A far-right leader pointed to neighborhoods with large immigrant populations, a prominent far-left politician blamed police tactics, and the government cited ultraleft agitators. But France’s longstanding commitment to colorblindness bars the state from collecting statistics on race and ethnicity, complicating efforts to understand the unrest. Stacy Meichtry and Bertrand Benoit write about the political taboo tearing France apart .

   5.   Welcome to the age of everything breaking.   Microsoft Outlook went dark. Air-traffic control grounded every departing U.S. flight. Then came outages at banks, airlines and even the National Security Agency. The failures appear to have different technical causes, but they underscore the vulnerabilities of our hyperconnected world, where aging systems and the race to fix security flaws pose growing challenges. In a darkly funny Saturday essay, Joel Stein explores why the bigger concern may not be the outages themselves, but our ability to recover from them —and how to get by when technology lets us down.

He has spent 113 days, or nearly 20% of his time in office, traveling abroad—more than twice as much time as President Trump over the same period. The globe-trotting is part of Carney’s push to forge new trade and security partnerships and reduce Canada’s reliance on the U.S. as Trump’s tariffs and annexation threats strain relations between the neighbors.

Now he is the unlikely literary sensation behind “Dungeon Crawler Carl,” a wildly popular fantasy series about a man in boxer shorts and a talking cat competing in a deadly alien game show. What began as a self-published series has sold more than 20 million copies and inspired men to read fiction en masse. Dinniman, who wrote the books in his underpants while eating Twizzlers, has become so famous that he is moving to a gated community, partly because fans keep knocking on his door.

Anthropic’s Rocky Debut Has Wall Street Pointing Fingers
 
Plus, the White House plans to scale back its use of ‘special government employees,’ and how to survive an age of widespread technology outages
 
 
 
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

What was supposed to be a triumphant week for Anthropic has devolved into a Wall Street blame game.

 

The company’s highly anticipated debut was meant to reassure investors about AI’s future. Instead, its shares fell 8.5% on its second day of trading Friday, wiping $109 billion from its market value. Now investors are questioning everything from who got shares to whether the opening price was set too high. The trouble goes well beyond Anthropic: Nasdaq stocks lost more than $4 trillion in value this week, erasing the index’s gains for the year.

 

Behind Anthropic’s debut are siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, who have built a company that prides itself on being anything but ordinary. Our reporters take you inside the brother-sister partnership at the top of what’s still one of the world’s most valuable companies.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• The White House plans to scale back its use of “special government employees,” who can work for the government while retaining their private-sector salaries or investments.

 

• New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch have forged an unlikely partnership that has helped keep crime low and reassured business and Jewish community leaders. Making it work has required compromises.

 

• A California jury found a man guilty of intentionally sparking the 2025 fire that devastated Los Angeles’s Pacific Palisades.

 

• Citadel Chief Executive Ken Griffin spent at least five years courting elite universities to bring a top technology school to Miami, hoping to turn his new home into a global business hub. He ultimately struck a $3 billion deal with Carnegie Mellon University.

 

• Denmark said it would expel Russia’s defense attaché after accusing Moscow of ordering the attempted killing of a Ukrainian-American rapper on Danish soil.

 

• Here’s a visual look at how El Salvador President Nayib Bukele is taking his gang-fighting strategy to Haiti.

 
 
 

3. FROM THE MARKETS

 

• Activist billionaire Nelson Peltz wants to take Wendy’s private. But the struggling burger chain’s CEO Bob Wright is standing in his way.

 
 
 

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

France’s riots are testing its colorblind ideals.

 

Student protests over school conditions spiraled into riots, setting off a fierce debate over who was responsible. A far-right leader pointed to neighborhoods with large immigrant populations, a prominent far-left politician blamed police tactics, and the government cited ultraleft agitators. But France’s longstanding commitment to colorblindness bars the state from collecting statistics on race and ethnicity, complicating efforts to understand the unrest. Stacy Meichtry and Bertrand Benoit write about the political taboo tearing France apart.

 

5.

 

Welcome to the age of everything breaking.

 

Microsoft Outlook went dark. Air-traffic control grounded every departing U.S. flight. Then came outages at banks, airlines and even the National Security Agency. The failures appear to have different technical causes, but they underscore the vulnerabilities of our hyperconnected world, where aging systems and the race to fix security flaws pose growing challenges. In a darkly funny Saturday essay, Joel Stein explores why the bigger concern may not be the outages themselves, but our ability to recover from them—and how to get by when technology lets us down.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Open offices have workers longing for cubicles.

 
 
 

As individual focus space continues to shrink across offices, we sat down with two designers to explore how floor plans could better support uninterrupted work. Watch the video to find out why you or your employees might be struggling to concentrate at work.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING THIS WEEKEND

 

• Saturday: NATO’s annual parliamentary assembly in Berlin. Formula One’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

 

• Sunday: The ATP Finals in Turin, Italy. The Philadelphia Marathon.

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
32
 

The number of countries Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has visited across five continents since taking office in March 2025. He has spent 113 days, or nearly 20% of his time in office, traveling abroad—more than twice as much time as President Trump over the same period. The globe-trotting is part of Carney’s push to forge new trade and security partnerships and reduce Canada’s reliance on the U.S. as Trump’s tariffs and annexation threats strain relations between the neighbors.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

He writes in his underwear. Now millions of men are reading his books.

 

Matt Dinniman used to sell cat-themed art on Etsy. Now he is the unlikely literary sensation behind “Dungeon Crawler Carl,” a wildly popular fantasy series about a man in boxer shorts and a talking cat competing in a deadly alien game show. What began as a self-published series has sold more than 20 million copies and inspired men to read fiction en masse. Dinniman, who wrote the books in his underpants while eating Twizzlers, has become so famous that he is moving to a gated community, partly because fans keep knocking on his door.

 
 
 

10. BEYOND THE NEWSROOM

 

• Opinion: The International Court of Justice issued a ruling designed to facilitate bad-faith allegations of “genocide” against Israel. The U.S. and its allies will also be in the cross-hairs soon enough.
